paragraphs: Zeus wakes up and orders Apollo to heal Hector, and the Trojans become victorious once more.

The Trojans fled past the trench and the set stakes, and many fell to the Danaans along the way. When they reached their chariots they halted, routed and pale with fear. Then Zeus woke on the crests of Ida, where he had been lying beside golden-throned Hera. He sprang to his feet and saw the Trojans and Achaeans. The Trojans were in confusion, and the Achaeans were driving them headlong before them, with King Poseidon among them. He saw Hector lying on the ground with his comrades gathered around him. Hector was gasping for breath, his mind wandering, and vomiting blood, for the man who had struck him was not the feeblest of the Achaeans.

The father of gods and men pitied Hector and glared at Hera. “I see it, Hera, you mischief-making trickster,” he said. “Your cunning has kept Hector from fighting and has routed his army. I am half inclined to thrash you, and you would be the first to reap the fruits of your scurvy knavery. Do you not remember the time I hung you up? I fastened two anvils to your feet and bound your hands in a golden chain that no one could break, and you dangled in mid-air among the clouds. All the gods of Olympus raged, but they could not get near enough to set you free. Any of them I caught, I seized and hurled from the heavenly threshold until he fell to earth half fainting. Even that did not ease my mind of its constant anxiety about noble Heracles. You and Boreas had spitefully carried him off across the seas to Cos, after you had won the tempests over to your scheme. But I rescued him, and in spite of all his mighty labors I brought him back to Argos. I remind you of this so that you will learn to stop your deceit, and see how much you are likely to gain from the embraces you left to come here and trick me.”

Hera trembled at his words. “Let heaven above and earth below be my witnesses,” she said, “and the waters of the river Styx—the most solemn oath a blessed god can take—and I swear also by your own almighty head and by our marriage bed, things I could never swear falsely by: Poseidon is not punishing Hector and the Trojans and helping the Achaeans because of anything I did. He acts entirely of his own accord, because he was sorry to see the Achaeans hard pressed at their ships. If I were advising him, I would tell him to do as you command.”

The father of gods and men smiled and answered, “Hera, if you always backed me when we sit in council of the gods, Poseidon, whether he liked it or not, would soon come round to your way of thinking and mine. So if you are telling the truth and mean what you say, go among the throng of the gods and tell Iris and Apollo, lord of the bow, that I want them. Iris is to go to the Achaean army and tell Poseidon to stop fighting and go home. Apollo is to send Hector back into battle and give him fresh strength. Hector will then forget his present sufferings and drive the Achaeans back in confusion, until they fall among the ships of Achilles son of Peleus. Achilles will then send his comrade Patroclus into battle. Hector will kill him in front of Ilium, after Patroclus has slain many warriors, among them my own noble son Sarpedon. To avenge Patroclus, Achilles will kill Hector. From that time on I will see to it that the Achaeans keep driving the Trojans back until Athena’s counsels are fulfilled and they take Ilium. But I will not give up my anger, and I will not let any god help the Danaans, until I have granted the wish of the son of Peleus. That is the promise I made, bowing my head, on the day Thetis touched my knees and begged me to give him honor.”

Hera heeded his words and went down from the heights of Ida to great Olympus. Her flight was as swift as a thought. A man’s fancy carries him over vast lands, and he says to himself, “Now I will be here, or there,” and wishes for all manner of things. That swiftly Hera flew until she reached high Olympus and entered the house of Zeus, where the gods were gathered. When they saw her, they all hurried to her and held out their cups in greeting. She ignored the others but took the cup from lovely Themis, who had been first to run up to her. “Hera,” Themis said, “why have you come? You seem troubled. Has your husband, the son of Cronus, been frightening you?”

Hera answered, “Themis, do not ask me about it. You know how proud and cruel my husband is. Take the gods to the feast, and there you and all the immortals will hear the wicked plans he has declared. Many, mortal and immortal, will be angered by them, however peacefully any of them may be feasting now.”

Hera sat down, and the gods throughout the house of Zeus were troubled. Laughter sat on her lips, but her brow was furrowed with care, and she spoke out in a rage. “What fools we are,” she cried, “to be so madly angry with Zeus! We keep wanting to go to him and stop him, by force or by persuasion, but he sits apart and cares for nobody, because he knows he is much stronger than any other immortal. So make the best of whatever evils he chooses to send each of you. Ares, I think, has already had a taste of them, for his son Ascalaphus has fallen in battle—the man he loved more dearly than any other, and whose father he admits himself to be.”

When Ares heard this, he struck his two sturdy thighs with the flat of his hands and said in anger, “Do not blame me, you gods who live in heaven, if I go to the ships of the Achaeans to avenge my son’s death, even if it ends with Zeus’s lightning striking me and I lie in blood and dust among the corpses.”

As he spoke he ordered his horses Panic and Rout to be yoked, and he put on his armor. Then Zeus would have been roused to fiercer and more implacable enmity against the other immortals, if Athena, alarmed for the safety of the gods, had not sprung from her seat and hurried outside. She tore the helmet from his head and the shield from his shoulders, took the bronze spear from his strong hand, and set it to one side. Then she said to Ares, “Madman, you are undone! Either you have ears that do not hear, or you have lost all judgment and understanding. Have you not heard what Hera said when she came straight from the presence of Olympian Zeus? Do you want to go through every kind of suffering before you are brought back to Olympus sick and sorry, after causing infinite mischief to the rest of us? Zeus would leave the Trojans and Achaeans to themselves at once. He would come to Olympus to punish us, and would grab us one after another, guilty or not. So give up your anger over your son’s death. Better men than he have been killed already or will fall hereafter, and one cannot protect everyone’s whole family.”

With these words she took Ares back to his seat. Meanwhile Hera called Apollo outside, together with Iris, the messenger of the gods. “Zeus,” she told them, “wants you to go to him on Mt. Ida at once. When you have seen him, you are to do whatever he then commands.”

Hera then left them and went back to her seat inside, while Iris and Apollo hurried on their way. They came to many-fountained Ida, mother of wild beasts, and found Zeus sitting on topmost Gargarus, a fragrant cloud wreathed around his head like a diadem. They stood before him. He was pleased that they had obeyed his wife’s orders so quickly.

He spoke to Iris first. “Go, swift Iris,” he said, “and give King Poseidon this message of mine—and tell him truly. He is to stop fighting and either join the company of the gods or go down into the sea. If he pays no attention and disobeys me, let him consider carefully whether he is strong enough to stand against me if I attack him. I am older and much stronger than he is. Yet he is not afraid to set himself up as my equal, though all the other gods stand in awe of me.”

Iris, swift as the wind, obeyed him. She sped down as swiftly as cold hail or snowflakes flying out of the clouds before the blast of Boreas, until she came close to the great shaker of the earth. Then she said, “O dark-haired king who holds the world in his embrace, I have come with a message from Zeus. He orders you to stop fighting and either join the company of the gods or go down into the sea. But if you pay no attention and disobey, he says he will come down here and fight you. He wants you to keep out of his reach, because he is older and much stronger than you are. Yet you are not afraid to set yourself up as his equal, though all the other gods stand in awe of him.”

Poseidon was very angry. “Great heavens!” he said. “Strong as Zeus may be, he has said more than he can do if he threatens violence against me, who am his equal in honor. We were three brothers whom Rhea bore to Cronus: Zeus, myself, and Hades, who rules the world below. Heaven and earth were divided three ways, and each of us was to have an equal share. When we cast lots, the sea fell to me as my dwelling forever. Hades took the darkness of the realms under the earth, while air and sky and clouds were the portion that fell to Zeus. But earth and great Olympus belong to all of us in common. So I will not walk as Zeus would have me. For all his strength, let him stay in his own third share and be content, without threatening to lay hands on me as though I were nobody. Let him save his bragging talk for his own sons and daughters, who have no choice but to obey him.”

Iris, swift as the wind, answered, “Poseidon, am I really to carry this bold and unyielding message to Zeus, or will you think again about your answer? Sensible people can be argued with, and you know that the Erinyes always take the side of the older person.”

Poseidon answered, “Goddess Iris, what you say is well timed. It is good when a messenger shows such discretion. Even so, it cuts me to the heart when anyone rebukes so angrily one who is his own peer and has equal power. Now, though, I will give way, in spite of my displeasure. And let me tell you something more, and I mean it: if Zeus spares steep Ilium and will not let the Achaeans have the great triumph of sacking it, against the wishes of me, Athena, driver of the spoil, Hera, Hermes, and King Hephaestus, then let him understand that he will bring on himself our implacable resentment.”

Poseidon then left the field and went down under the sea, and the Achaeans sorely missed him. Zeus then said to Apollo, “Dear Phoebus, go to Hector. Poseidon, who holds the earth in his embrace, has gone down under the sea to escape the severity of my anger. If he had not, the gods below with Cronus would have heard of the fight between us. It is better for both of us that he curbed his anger and kept out of my reach, for I would have had much trouble with him. Now take your tasseled aegis and shake it furiously to throw the Achaean heroes into a panic. And take brave Hector into your own care, O Far-Darter, and rouse him to daring deeds until the Achaeans are sent flying back to their ships and the Hellespont. From there I will think the matter over, and decide how the Achaeans may get a respite from their troubles.”

Apollo did as his father said. He left the crests of Ida and flew down like a falcon, the swiftest of all birds and the bane of doves. Hector was no longer lying on the ground. He was sitting up, having just come to himself, and he recognized the men around him. The sweat and the hard breathing had left him the moment the will of aegis-bearing Zeus revived him. Apollo stood beside him and asked, “Hector son of Priam, why are you so faint, and why are you sitting here apart from the others? Has some mishap befallen you?”

Hector answered in a weak voice, “Which of the gods are you, kind sir, to ask me this? Do you not know that Ajax struck me on the chest with a stone while I was killing his comrades at the ships of the Achaeans, and made me stop fighting? I was sure that this very day I would breathe my last and go down into the house of Hades.”

Then King Apollo said to him, “Take heart. The son of Cronus has sent you a mighty helper from Ida to stand by you and defend you: I, Phoebus Apollo of the golden sword, who have guarded not only you but your city until now. So order your horsemen to drive their chariots to the ships in great numbers. I will go ahead of your horses and smooth the way for them, and I will turn the Achaeans in flight.”

As he spoke he filled the shepherd of his people with great strength. A horse that has been stabled and well fed breaks loose and gallops gloriously across the plain to the place where he is used to bathing in the river. He tosses his head, his mane streams over his shoulders, and in all the pride of his strength he flies at full speed to the pastures where the mares are feeding. So Hector, when he heard the god’s words, urged his horsemen on and rushed forward as fast as his limbs could carry him. Or think of country peasants who set their hounds on a horned stag or wild goat. It has taken shelter under a rock or thicket, and they cannot find it, but then a bearded lion, roused by their shouts, stands in their path, and they have no more heart for the chase. So the Achaeans had been charging on in a body, using their swords and spears pointed at both ends, but when they saw Hector going about among his men they were afraid, and their hearts fell down into their feet.

Then Thoas son of Andraemon, leader of the Aetolians, spoke. He was a man who could make a good throw, staunch in close fight, and few could surpass him in debate when opinions were divided. With complete sincerity and goodwill he addressed them: “In heaven’s name, what do I see? Is that not Hector, come to life again? Everyone was sure he had been killed by Ajax son of Telamon, but it seems one of the gods has rescued him again. He has already killed many of us Danaans, and I think he will go on doing so, for the hand of Zeus must be with him, or he would never dare show himself so masterful in the forefront of the battle. So let us all do as I say. Let us order the main body of our forces to fall back on the ships. But those of us who claim to be the flower of the army should stand firm and see whether we can hold Hector back with the points of our spears as soon as he comes near us. I expect that he will then think better of it before he tries to charge into the press of the Danaans.”

So he spoke, and they did exactly as he had said. Those around Ajax and King Idomeneus, along with the followers of Teucer, Meriones, and Meges, peer of Ares, called all their best men about them and held the fight against Hector and the Trojans. The main body fell back on the ships of the Achaeans.

The Trojans came on in a dense body, and Hector strode at their head. Phoebus Apollo walked in front of him, with cloud wrapped around his shoulders. In his hands he carried the terrible aegis, shaggy with fringe, that Hephaestus the smith had made for Zeus to strike terror into men’s hearts. Holding it, Apollo led the Trojans on.

The Argives held together and stood their ground. The battle cry rose high from both sides, and arrows flew from the bowstrings. Many a spear sped from strong hands and fastened in the bodies of valiant warriors, while others dropped to earth midway, before they could taste man’s fair flesh and glut themselves with blood. As long as Phoebus Apollo held his aegis quietly, without shaking it, the weapons on both sides struck home and men fell. But when he shook it straight in the Danaans’ faces and raised his mighty battle cry, their hearts fainted within them and they forgot their former prowess. Two wild beasts spring in the dead of night on a herd of cattle or a large flock of sheep when the herdsman is not there. In the same way the Danaans were struck helpless, for Apollo filled them with panic and gave victory to Hector and the Trojans.

The fighting grew more scattered after that, and each man killed whomever he could. Hector killed Stichius and Arcesilaus, one a leader of the Boeotians and the other a friend and comrade of Menestheus. Aeneas killed Medon and Iasus. Medon was a bastard son of Oileus and a brother of Ajax. He lived in Phylace, away from his own country, because he had killed a kinsman of his stepmother Eriopis, whom Oileus had married. Iasus had become a leader of the Athenians and was the son of Sphelus, the son of Boucolos. Polydamas killed Mecisteus, and Polites killed Echius, both in the front of the battle, while Agenor slew Clonius. Paris struck Deiochus from behind, low on the shoulder, as he fled among the foremost fighters, and the spear point went clean through him.

While they were stripping these heroes of their armor, the Achaeans fled headlong to the trench and the set stakes and were forced back inside their wall. Hector then shouted to the Trojans, “Forward to the ships, and leave the spoils! If I see any man hanging back on the far side of the wall, away from the ships, I will have him killed. His kinsmen and kinswomen will not give him his due of fire; dogs will tear him to pieces in front of our city.”

As he spoke he laid his whip across his horses’ shoulders and called to the Trojans all along their ranks. The Trojans shouted with a cry that rent the air and kept their horses neck and neck with his. Phoebus Apollo went ahead and kicked the banks of the deep trench down into its middle, making a great broad bridge, as wide as a spear’s throw when a man is testing his strength. The Trojan battalions poured over the bridge, with Apollo and his formidable aegis leading the way. He kicked down the wall of the Achaeans as easily as a child kicks down a house of sand that he has built, playing on the sea shore, and so destroys it. In the same way, O Apollo, you poured toil and trouble on the Argives, filling them with panic and confusion.

So the Achaeans were hemmed in at their ships, calling out to one another and raising their hands to heaven with loud cries, every man of them. Nestor of Gerene, tower of strength to the Achaeans, lifted his hands to the starry firmament of heaven and prayed more fervently than any. “Father Zeus,” he said, “if anyone in wheat-growing Argos ever burned you the fat thigh-bones of a sheep or heifer and prayed to return safely home, and you bowed your head to him in assent, remember it now. Do not let the Trojans triumph over the Achaeans like this.”

All-counseling Zeus thundered loudly in answer to the prayer of the aged son of Neleus. When the Trojans heard Zeus thunder, they flung themselves still more fiercely on the Achaeans. A wave breaks over the bulwarks of a ship when the sea runs high before a gale—the force of the wind is what makes the waves so great. In the same way the Trojans sprang over the wall with a shout and drove their chariots onward. The two sides fought hand to hand with their double-pointed spears, the Trojans from their chariots, and the Achaeans from up in their ships, wielding the long pikes that lay on the decks ready for a sea fight, jointed and shod with bronze.
